# State-space models {#ssm}

This chapter describes how to write a state-space model (SSM) in an ilike file. Here we reintroduce the concept, following the description in section \@ref(inference-pf). An SSM describes the evolution of an indirectly observed latent "state" variable over time. We denote the state at time $t$ as $x_t$ and the observation at time $t$ as $y_t$. A Markov assumption is made on the state, so that the distribution of $x_t$ depends only on $x_{t-1}$. A further conditional independence assumption is made that $y_t$ is conditionally independent of all other variables in the system given $x_t$. The distribution of $x_t$ given $x_{t-1}$ is known as the transition/dynamic model, with the distribution of $y_t$ given $x_t$ being known as the measurement/observation model. The specification of a joint distribution over variables $x_{0:T}$ and $y_{0:T}$, for some final time $T$, is completed by a prior on $x_0$, the initial state.

Several different types of inference tasks are specific to SSMs: e.g. filtering, smoothing and prediction of the latent state. ilike currently supports filtering, by Kalman filters (`KF`), particle filters (`PF`) and ensemble Kalman filters (`EnKF`), and the estimate of the marginal likelihood that a filter gives can be used as the likelihood of the model's parameters (section \@ref(algorithmic-likelihood)).

## Writing a state-space model

An SSM is written in the model section with four kinds of statement:

```{r, echo=FALSE, comment=""}
cat(readLines("examples/language/ssm.ilike"), sep = "\n")
```

- **The prior on the initial state** $x_0$ is a prior, written as in chapter \@ref(models): here `x ~ norm(0, 1)`. The Kalman filter requires it to be a simple Gaussian prior (`x ~ norm(…)` or `x ~ mvnorm(…)`).
- **The transition model** $x_t \mid x_{t-1}$ is written `transition x = …`, where `x` is the state (section \@ref(transition-models)).
- **The measurement model** $y_t \mid x_t$ is a likelihood factor, written as in chapter \@ref(models). If several likelihood factors are given, the observed variables in each are assumed to be conditionally independent given $x_t$. The Kalman and ensemble Kalman filters take such factors one after another at each time (each update starting from the previous one), which gives the same result as one factor holding all the observed variables; the ensemble Kalman filter requires each of them to be a Gaussian data model. It can also be a model statement such as `y ~ norm(x, 1)`. Then `y` must be data: either given in the file's data section, or declared there (`data { vector y }`) when the data come from the file that runs the filter, as for `pf(inner)` (section \@ref(algorithmic-likelihood)). A model statement on a variable that is not data and whose distribution reads the state is refused, since it would make `y` a parameter rather than the measurement. The Kalman and ensemble Kalman filters require Gaussian data models (section \@ref(gaussian-data-models)).
- **The time index** is written `time = ssm(…)` (section \@ref(time-index)).

The data are given in the data section, with one row per time: the measurement at index $t$ is row $t$ of each data variable, counting from 0 (so, with `first_index = 0`, the first row is the measurement at time 0). A vector of data is one measurement per time; a matrix has one row per time and one column for each dimension of the measurement.

With these, the file can be run with any of the filters, each in its own algorithm section:

```{r,eval=FALSE}
recipe = compile("ssm.ilike")
KF(recipe, algorithm = "kf", results_name = "kf")
PF(recipe, algorithm = "pf", results_name = "pf", seed = 1)
EnKF(recipe, algorithm = "enkf", results_name = "enkf", seed = 1)
```

Each returns the log of the estimated (for the KF, exact) marginal likelihood $\log p(y_{0:T})$.

## The time index {#time-index}

`time = ssm(…)` gives the index of the SSM and how it relates to the times of the data:

`ssm(index, first_index, last_index, time, initial_time, time_difference, time_step, predictions_per_update)`

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `index` | a name for the variable that indexes the SSM, i.e the $t$ in $x_t$ |
| `first_index` | the first index, i.e. the $0$ in $x_0$ |
| `last_index` | the last index, i.e. the $T$ in $x_T$ |
| `time` | a name for the variable holding the time of each observation. This need not be the same as the index: this is useful if the sampling frequency of the data is not 1 |
| `initial_time` | the time of the first observation |
| `time_difference` | a name for the variable holding the time difference between observations |
| `time_step` | the time step between states of the SSM |
| `predictions_per_update` | the number of times the transition model is used between observations (more than 1 when, for example, the transition model is an SDE solver with a small time step) |

The arguments may also be given in order: `time = ssm(i, 0, 4, t, 0, dt, 1, 1)`. The variables named by `index`, `time` and `time_difference` are passed to the transition model, the transition proposal and the data model with the parameters (`parameters["i"]` in C++), set for the time being proposed, so that the models can depend on time. The `predictions_per_update` uses of the transition model between two observations all see the values for the observation they lead to. This holds for all the filters, including the Kalman filter, whose matrices and covariances may be functions of the time.

## Transition models {#transition-models}

### Linear-Gaussian transition

```
transition x = linear_gaussian(matrix = A, covariance = Q)
```

gives the transition
$$
x_t \sim \mathcal{N}(A x_{t-1}, Q),
(\#eq:lgtm)
$$
where $A$ is a matrix and $Q$ is a covariance matrix. Each may be numbers (`matrix = 0.9`, `covariance = [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]]`) or a function returning a matrix, which may depend on the parameters (`arma::mat f(const Parameters &parameters)` in C++; see the example in section \@ref(algorithmic-likelihood)). The arguments may also be given in order: `linear_gaussian(0.9, 0.5)`. The Kalman filter requires a linear-Gaussian transition.

A filter evaluates the transition's matrix and covariance for every particle at every time step. A covariance given as numbers is factorised once. When they are functions that depend only on parameters, declaring which ones lets a filter compute them once per run instead: `linear_gaussian(matrix = cpp::A, covariance = cpp::Q, reads = [a, s])` says that `A` and `Q` read only the parameters `a` and `s`. At the start of each run, the filter evaluates them with only `a` and `s` available, so a function that reads anything else stops with a message; during the run it uses those values for every particle whose `a` and `s` are the ones it computed them with (and computes them again otherwise). `reads` may not name the state or the variables of `time = ssm(...)`, whose values change within a run. With a 10-dimensional state, this cut the time of a particle marginal Metropolis–Hastings run whose covariance depended on a parameter by about 40%.

### Nonlinear-Gaussian transition

```
transition x = nonlinear_gaussian(function = cpp::f, covariance = Q)
```

gives the transition
$$
x_t \sim \mathcal{N}(f(x_{t-1}), Q),
$$
where $f$ is a function of the state (and parameters) returning the predicted state: `Parameters f(const Parameters &parameters)` in C++. The covariance is given as for the linear-Gaussian transition, and `reads = [...]` declares the parameters a covariance function reads, in the same way.

### A built-in random walk

```
transition x = norm_rw(x, 0.5)
```

gives a random walk on the state, using one of the random walks of section \@ref(mcmc-proposals) (`norm_rw`, `mvnorm_rw`, `unif_rw`, `mvunif_rw`); the state may be left out (`norm_rw(0.5)`).

### A transition written as functions

```
transition x = density(simulate = cpp::simulate_state, log = cpp::log_transition)
```

gives a transition written by the user:

- `simulate` simulates the state at time $t$ given the state at time $t-1$ and any parameters that the model relies on: `Parameters f(RandomNumberGenerator &rng, const Parameters &parameters)` in C++, where `parameters` holds $x_{t-1}$ and the parameters, and the function returns $x_t$;
- `log` evaluates the log transition density: `double f(const Parameters &proposed_parameters, const Parameters &parameters)`, with $x_t$ in `proposed_parameters` and $x_{t-1}$ in `parameters`.

Only the functions required by the chosen inference algorithm need be given: for example, the bootstrap particle filter does not evaluate the density of the transition model, so `log` may be left out.

## Transition proposals {#transition-proposal}

A particle filter moves its particles from time $t-1$ to time $t$ using a *transition proposal*. If none is given, the transition model is used as the proposal, yielding the bootstrap filter of @gordon1993novel. A proposal that also uses the measurement at time $t$ (a "guided" proposal) can give a much better estimate of the likelihood. It is given in the algorithm section, by `transition_proposal`:

```{r, echo=FALSE, comment=""}
cat(readLines("examples/language/ssm_guided.ilike"), sep = "\n")
```

- `simulate` simulates the state at time $t$: `Parameters f(RandomNumberGenerator &rng, const Parameters &parameters, const Data &data)` in C++, where `parameters` holds $x_{t-1}$ and the parameters, including the index variable of the SSM (here `i`), set to the index of the time $t$ being proposed, together with the time and time-difference variables; and `data` holds the data at time $t$: the measurement(s) of the time being proposed (`data["y"]` is $y_t$, not the whole series).
- `log` evaluates the log density of the proposal: `double f(const Parameters &proposed_parameters, const Parameters &parameters, const Data &data)`.

A particle filter with a transition proposal evaluates the transition model's density in its weights, so the transition model must then have `log` (or be one of the built-in transitions).
